I have this crazy theory that as folks who care about safety start buying self driving cars, the dumbasses driving unsafely will start causing more accidents.

It's basically: if the self driving car is actually following traffic laws and driving safely, an impatient driver is going to have a higher likelihood of doing shitty things to "get around them." Imagine the roads full of timid and well educated but freshly minted drivers training drivers.

I was just talking to my coworker about this. When self driving cars are the norm, you're going to see a rise in accidents by humans assuming other cars won't drive aggressively. Two manually driven cars both intentionally driving into an intersection at a four way stop without right of way, for example, assuming that the cautious AI in the other cars won't hit them. What's more disconcerting is what will happen to pedestrians who will start to view crossing roads as safer, when paired with human drivers being more aggressive in intersections?

Okay, yes the car was rear ended, but the reason it was rear ended doesn't necessarily mean that the other driver was irresponsible. Most reports of the self driving cars say that they are safe, but often at stop signs, they will repeatedly edge forward, then stop. This is very unpredictable behavior. If you are turning right, and the car in front of you starts to go, you will start to look left to see if you can go. If the car in front of you makes a quick stop again for no reason, it is surprising and you might hit them. The cars might drive safely, but they don't drive predictably. They don't adhere to the "norms" of most drivers, and so it is difficult to predict what they will do, making it difficult to share the road with them.

There are two types of astronauts. Pilot astronauts and mission specialists.

Pilot astronauts have a ridiculous combination of skills, and most are experienced fighter pilots (preferably test pilots) who also have hard science PhDs. There aren't many people who fit this bill.

Mission specialists can be pretty much anyone with a PhD in anything vaguely useful-sounding. I'm sure they're all very good, but there's a much larger candidate pool in this category.

So it should come as no surprise that NASA picks the best-qualified pilot astronauts first, inevitably says "Oops, they're all white dudes" and then fills the mission specialist roles with "other groups" just for diversity.
